quotes.t: I hope I will be able to confide everything to you, as I have never been able to confide in anyone, and I hope you will be a great source of comfort and support.

I see the eight of us in the Annex as if we were a patch of blue sky surrounded by menacing black clouds. The perfectly round spot on which we're standing is still safe, but the clouds are moving in on us.
I long to ride a bike, dance, whistle, look at the world, feel young and know that I'm free, and yet I can't let it show.
I wander from room to room, climb up and down the stairs and feel like a songbird whose wings have been ripped off and who keeps hurling itself against the bars of its dark cage.
We are each made for goodness, love and compassion. Our lives are transformed as much as the world is when we live with these truths.
The God who existed before any religion counts on you to make the oneness of the human family known and celebrated.
Isn't it amazing that we are all made in God's image, and yet there is so much diversity among his people?
When we see the face of a child, we think of the future. We think of their dreams about what they might become, and what they might accomplish.
I watched life and wanted to be a part of it but found it painfully difficult.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 1: 1931-1934

quotes.t: Anything I can not transform into something marvelous, I let go. Reality doesn't impress me.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 1: 1931-1934

quotes.t: I only believe in intoxication, in ecstasy, and when ordinary life shackles me, I escape, one way or another. No more walls.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 2: 1934-1939

quotes.t: I hate men who are afraid of women's strength.
quotes.source: A Journal of Love: The Unexpurgated Diary, 1931-1932

quotes.t: Bitter for a free man is the bondage of debt.
Adversity shows whether we have friends, or only the shadows of friends.
Whom Fortune wishes to destroy she first makes mad.
No man who has once heartily and wholly laughed can be altogether irreclaimably bad.
Man's unhappiness, as I construe, comes of his greatness; it is because there is an Infinite in him, which with all his cunning he cannot quite bury under the Finite.
That there should one Man die ignorant who had capacity for Knowledge, this I call a tragedy.
As a woman I have no country. As a woman I want no country. As a woman my country is the whole world.
Women have served all these centuries as looking glasses possessing the magic and delicious power of reflecting the figure of man at twice its natural size.
It would have been impossible, completely and entirely, for any woman to have written the plays of Shakespeare in the age of Shakespeare.
Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin.

So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein—more, far more, will I achieve: treading in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and unfold to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.
With how many things are we on the brink of becoming acquainted, if cowardice or carelessness did not restrain our inquiries.
The imagination may be compared to Adam's dream — he awoke and found it truth.
A man's life of any worth is a continual allegory — and very few eyes can see the mystery of life — a life like the Scriptures, figurative.
The genius of poetry must work out its own salvation in a man; it cannot be matured by law and precept, but by sensation and watchfulness in itself.
quotes.source: Letter to J. H. Reynolds, 3 February 1818

quotes.t: You have to trust in something — your gut, destiny, life, karma, whatever. This approach has never let me down, and it has made all the difference in my life.
Because believing that the dots will connect down the road will give you the confidence to follow your heart, even when it leads you off the well-worn path.
If you haven't found it yet, keep looking — and don't settle.

I prefer Buddhism because it gives three principles in combination, which no other religion does. Buddhism teaches prajna (understanding as against superstition and supernaturalism), karuna (love), and samata (equality). This is what man wants for a good and happy life. Neither god nor soul can save society.
quotes.source: Why I like Buddhism and how it is useful to the world in its present circumstances (BBC radio talk, May 1956)

quotes.t: In every country the intellectual class is the most influential class. This is the class which can foresee, advise and lead.
quotes.source: Speech delivered to the Bombay Presidency Mahar Conference, 31 May 1936

quotes.t: History bears out the proposition that political revolutions have always been preceded by social and religious revolutions.
The transformation of the world is brought about by the transformation of oneself.
Without love the acquisition of knowledge only increases confusion and leads to self-destruction.
quotes.source: Education and the Significance of Life (1953)

quotes.t: And as we are — the world is. That is, if we are greedy, envious, competitive, our society will be competitive, envious, greedy, which brings misery and war. The State is what we are.
quotes.source: Second Public Talk at Ojai, 21 May 1944

quotes.t: Freedom cannot be bestowed — it must be achieved.
quotes.source: Little Journeys for 1908 (essay on Booker T. Washington)

quotes.t: If men will not act for themselves, what will they do when the benefit of their effort is for all?
Responsibilities gravitate to the person who can shoulder them.
quotes.source: "J.B. Runs Things," Elbert Hubbard's Selected Writings, Part 14 (1923)

quotes.t: Enlighten the people generally, and tyranny and oppressions of body and mind will vanish like evil spirits at the dawn of day.
quotes.source: Letter to Pierre Samuel Du Pont de Nemours, 24 April 1816

quotes.t: Question with boldness even the existence of a God; because, if there be one, he must more approve of the homage of reason, than that of blindfolded fear.

A wise and frugal Government, which shall restrain men from injuring one another, shall leave them otherwise free to regulate their own pursuits of industry and improvement, and shall not take from the mouth of labor the bread it has earned.
Whatever happens I have had these blissful, perfect moments and they are worth living for.
quotes.source: Letter to Richard Murry, January 1920 (The Letters of Katherine Mansfield, Vol. II)

quotes.t: To work — to work! It is such infinite delight to know that we still have the best things to do.
quotes.source: Letter to Bertrand Russell, 7 December 1916 (The Collected Letters of Katherine Mansfield, Vol. I)

quotes.t: Looking back, I imagine I was always writing. Twaddle it was too. But better far write twaddle or anything, anything, than nothing at all.
quotes.source: Journal entry, July 1922 (The Journal of Katherine Mansfield, 1927)

quotes.t: To put it briefly, we possess nothing that isn't mortal, except the benefits of the heart and the mind.
But of a surety man's last day must ever be awaited, and none be counted happy till his death, till his last funeral rites are paid.
quotes.source: Metamorphoses, Book 3 (lines 135-137), trans. Frank Justus Miller

quotes.t: Poor me! Love cannot be cured by herbs.
A ruffled mind makes a restless pillow.
Better to be without logic than without feeling.
If all the world hated you, and believed you wicked, while your own conscience approved you, and absolved you from guilt, you would not be without friends.

Find out just what any people will quietly submit to and you have found out the exact measure of injustice and wrong which will be imposed upon them, and these will continue till they are resisted with either words or blows, or with both.
Slaves are generally expected to sing as well as to work.
Every tone was a testimony against slavery, and a prayer to God for deliverance from chains.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

quotes.t: Has any one supposed it lucky to be born? I hasten to inform him or her it is just as lucky to die, and I know it.
quotes.source: Song of Myself, section 7, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: Behold, I do not give lectures or a little charity, When I give I give myself.
quotes.source: Song of Myself, section 40, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: Now I see the secret of the making of the best persons, It is to grow in the open air and to eat and sleep with the earth.
quotes.source: Song of the Open Road, section 6, Leaves of Grass

quotes.t: No one is so old as to think that he may not live a year.
What the object of senile avarice may be I cannot conceive. For can there be anything more absurd than to seek more journey money, the less there remains of the journey?
The foundation of justice, moreover, is good faith, that is, truth and fidelity to promises and agreements.
An intelligent, energetic, educated woman cannot be kept in four walls — even satin-lined, diamond-studded walls — without discovering sooner or later that they are still a prison cell.
Acceptance of the unacceptable is the greatest source of grace in this world.
A good upbringing means not that you won't spill sauce on the tablecloth, but that you won't notice it when someone else does.

When your determination changes, everything else will begin to move in the direction you desire. The moment you resolve to be victorious, every nerve and fiber in your being will immediately orient itself toward your success.
I don't count my sit-ups. I only start counting when it starts hurting because they're the only ones that count.
The greatest of all mistakes is to do nothing because you think you can only do a little.
The old order changeth, yielding place to new.
We don't know a millionth of one percent about anything.
If you are not willing to risk the usual, you will have to settle for the ordinary.
First principle: never to let one's self be beaten down by persons or by events.
The stock market is a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient.
I believe in being strong when everything seems to be going wrong. I believe that happy girls are the prettiest girls. I believe that tomorrow is another day, and I believe in miracles.
quotes.source: Statement accepting the Screen Actors Guild Achievement Award, January 1993

quotes.t: You, the people, have the power to make this life free and beautiful, to make this life a wonderful adventure.
It isn't what you have or who you are or where you are or what you are doing that makes you happy or unhappy. It is what you think about it.
quotes.source: How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936)

quotes.t: He that will not apply new remedies must expect new evils; for time is the greatest innovator.
Depend upon it, sir, when a man knows he is to be hanged in a fortnight, it concentrates his mind wonderfully.
quotes.source: Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson (1791)

quotes.t: Show me someone without an ego, and I'll show you a loser.
We judge ourselves by what we feel capable of doing, while others judge us by what we have already done.
A man should never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong, which is but saying, in other words, that he is wiser today than he was yesterday.
No testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish.
Remember that wherever your heart is, there you will find your treasure.
If you want to know what a man's like, take a good look at how he treats his inferiors, not his equals.
quotes.source: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2000)

quotes.t: There is not a liberal America and a conservative America — there is the United States of America.
quotes.source: Keynote Address at the 2004 Democratic National Convention

quotes.t: I don't like to lose — at anything — yet I've grown most not from victories, but setbacks.
None can destroy iron, but its own rust can. Likewise, none can destroy a person, but his own mindset can.
I have found that the way of the warrior is death.
The dew of the rouge-flower, when it is spilled, is simply water.
No help for the likes of me, I go on walking.
Tea with us became more than an idealisation of the form of drinking; it is a religion of the art of life.
For all that has been — Thanks. For all that shall be — Yes.
I love Thee with two loves — love for my own happiness, and perfect love, to love Thee as is Thy due.
Imagine one thousand suns in the sky at the same time.
Reason is immortal, all else mortal.
I saw my Lord with the eye of my heart, and I said: "Who are You?" He said: "You."
People are the castle, people are the stone walls, people are the moat.
One star for my memory, one star for my love, one star for my loneliness, one star for my longing, one star for my poems, one star for my mother, my mother.
Happiness resides not in possessions, and not in gold, happiness dwells in the soul.
Come, let us all be friends for once, let us make life easy on us, let us be lovers and loved ones, the earth shall be left to no one.

If God asked me what my wish was, I would reply unhesitatingly, "Korean independence." If he asked me what my second wish was, I would again answer, "My country's independence." If he asked me what my third wish was, I would reply in an even louder voice, "My wish is the complete independence of my country, Korea."
Truth and love must prevail over lies and hatred.

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Audrey Hepburn.bio: Audrey Hepburn was a British actress and humanitarian celebrated for films such as Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady. In later life she devoted herself to UNICEF, serving as a Goodwill Ambassador in some of the world's poorest regions.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Barack Obama.bio: 44th president of the United States (2009-2017), the first African American to hold the office; Nobel Peace Prize 2009.

Charlie Chaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin was an English comic actor and filmmaker whose Little Tramp became a global icon of silent cinema. He co-founded United Artists and wrote, directed and starred in classics including City Lights, Modern Times and The Great Dictator.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Chiyo-ni.bio: Chiyo-ni was a Japanese haiku poet of the Edo period, one of the most celebrated women in the form. Her famous morning-glory haiku — giving up her well water rather than harm the vine — is known throughout Japan.

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Dag Hammarskjöld.bio: Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish diplomat who served as the second Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1953 until his death in a plane crash during a peace mission to the Congo. He was posthumously awarded the Nobel Peace Prize; his spiritual journal Markings was published after his death.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Dale Carnegie.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and lecturer on self-improvement and public speaking. His book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) became one of the best-selling books of all time.

David Hume.bio: David Hume was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher, historian and economist, best known for A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding. His scepticism about causation, miracles and the self profoundly influenced Western philosophy.

Democritus.bio: Democritus was a Greek philosopher who, with Leucippus, developed the atomic theory of the universe. He held that reality consists of indivisible atoms moving in empty space, and was known in antiquity as the laughing philosopher.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Donald Trump.bio: Donald Trump is an American businessman and television personality who served as the 45th President of the United States (2017–2021) and was elected again as the 47th President in 2024. Before politics he built a real-estate business and hosted the reality show The Apprentice.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Francis Bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman and essayist who championed the empirical method of inquiry. His Essays and his plan for the reform of learning in the Novum Organum helped lay the groundwork of modern science.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

J.K. Rowling.bio: British author (1965– ), creator of Harry Potter.

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Kim Gu.bio: Kim Gu was a leader of the Korean independence movement and head of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in exile. His memoir Baekbeom Ilji dreams of a Korea that is not the richest or strongest nation, but the most beautiful.

Mansur al-Hallaj.bio: Persian Sufi mystic executed in Baghdad for his ecstatic declaration 'Ana al-Haqq' (I am the Truth).

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Okakura Kakuzo.bio: Okakura Kakuzo was a Japanese scholar who worked to preserve Japan's traditional arts and explained Asian culture to the West. His Book of Tea (1906), written in English, remains a classic meditation on simplicity and beauty.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Paulo Coelho.bio: Brazilian lyricist and novelist whose novel The Alchemist became one of the best-selling books in history, translated into dozens of languages. His fables about following one's dreams have inspired readers on every continent.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Pythagoras.bio: Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher and mathematician who founded a religious and philosophical community in southern Italy. He is remembered for the theorem that bears his name and for teachings on number, harmony and the disciplined life.

Rabia al-Adawiyya.bio: Muslim saint and Sufi mystic of Basra, one of the earliest voices of divine love in Islamic mysticism.

Ratan Tata.role: Industrialist, chairman emeritus of Tata Sons
Ratan Tata.bio: Chairman of Tata Sons for more than two decades, Ratan Tata transformed the Tata group into a global conglomerate with acquisitions such as Tetley, Corus and Jaguar Land Rover. Revered in India for his integrity and philanthropy, he also championed the Tata Nano, the world's cheapest car.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Santoka Taneda.bio: Santoka Taneda was a Japanese Zen monk and free-verse haiku poet who wandered the country on foot for years, begging his way from temple to temple. His spare poems record mountains, rain, and sake with disarming honesty.

Serena Williams.bio: American tennis legend who won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most in the Open Era, along with four Olympic gold medals. Born in Saginaw, Michigan, and raised in Compton, California, she dominated women's tennis for over two decades and became a successful businesswoman and advocate for women.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Takeda Shingen.bio: Takeda Shingen was a Japanese daimyo of the Sengoku period, one of the era's most feared and capable warlords. His battle standard bore the famous Fūrinkazan motto from Sun Tzu: fast as the wind, silent as a forest, fierce as fire, immovable as a mountain.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Václav Havel.bio: Václav Havel was a Czech playwright and dissident who became the first president of post-communist Czechoslovakia and then of the Czech Republic. His essays, especially The Power of the Powerless, articulated the moral resistance of living in truth under totalitarianism.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Warren Buffett.bio: Investor Warren Buffett, the 'Oracle of Omaha', turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the world's largest conglomerates through patient, disciplined value investing. Famous for his annual shareholder letters and frugal personal habits, he has pledged to give away the great majority of his fortune.

Yamamoto Tsunetomo.bio: Yamamoto Tsunetomo was a Japanese samurai of the Nabeshima clan whose spoken reflections were recorded as the Hagakure, a guide to the way of the warrior centered on devotion and living fully in the present moment.

Yoko Ono.bio: Yoko Ono is a Japanese artist, musician, and peace activist, a pioneer of conceptual art whose instruction pieces in Grapefruit invited audiences to complete the work in their imagination. She was married to John Lennon.

Yun Dong-ju.bio: Yun Dong-ju was a Korean poet who wrote lyrical, conscience-stricken verse under Japanese colonial rule. Arrested for independence activities, he died in a Fukuoka prison at twenty-eight; his poem 'Foreword' is known to every Korean schoolchild.

Yunus Emre.bio: Turkish folk poet and Sufi, a central voice of Anatolian humanism writing in simple, powerful Turkish verse.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
